#6150. Texas Republicans’ gerrymander backfires as Democrats gain ground in U.S. House delegation

This article originally appeared on The Texas Tribune.

In 2025, Texas Republicans, pushed by President Donald Trump, redrew the state’s congressional map before the midterms, converting five Democratic-held districts into ones Trump would have carried by at least 10 percentage points.

The move backfired: GOP candidates lost four of five seats their new congressional map was designed to flip and lost two of their own.

That means Texas Republicans will head to Washington in January with 24 U.S. House seats, one less than they had at the start of the current Congress. When the state Legislature in Austin pursued the controversial mid-decade gerrymander, Republicans had hoped for a 30-8 split in the delegation but will end up instead at 24-14.

In South Texas, moderate Democratic Reps. Henry Cuellar of Laredo and Vicente Gonzalez of McAllen both won reelection, surviving the redraw that put more Trump voters in their districts. Republicans also lost ground in the lone Rio Grande Valley district they already held, as Tejano musician Bobby Pulido ousted two-term Rep. Monica De La Cruz, R-Edinburg.

Democrats picked up another seat with Katy Padilla Stout’s win over YouTuber and gun-rights activist Brandon Herrera in the 23rd Congressional District, a sprawling seat covering San Antonio to the outskirts of El Paso. The district has been vacant since former GOP Rep. Tony Gonzales resigned in April over a sex scandal with a staffer. Despite the district’s 15-point lean for Trump, Padilla Stout, a San Antonio attorney and former teacher, made it onto the radar of national Democrats who saw opportunity in the district’s majority-Hispanic status and Herrera’s history of edgy, controversial comments.

Democrats held fast to districts elsewhere, despite their incumbents being displaced due to the redraw. In the San Antonio area, Bexar County sheriff’s deputy Johnny Garcia beat Republican Carlos De La Cruz, the brother of Monica De La Cruz, in the newly crafted 35th Congressional District, a GOP target that Trump carried by 10 points.

In Houston, the grassroots campaign of Democrat Leticia Gutierrez topped Army veteran and former investment banker Alex Mealer, despite being vastly outspent in a district that Trump won by 20 percentage points two years ago. Gutierrez raised just a fraction of Mealer’s $2.8 million haul over the midterm cycle, as of mid-October, according to Federal Election Commission filings.

Republicans had high hopes for the redraw, which Democrats fought by fleeing the state, keeping the map in limbo by temporarily denying Republicans the headcount to pass it. But the new lines could not withstand the blue wave that swept through much of the country Tuesday, driven in part by the leftward swing of Latino voters. Texas’ new map banked on the GOP holding most of Trump’s 2024 gains with Latino Texans, who made up a majority of the eligible voting population in four of the five targets.

Nor did the redraw deliver what the White House wanted from it: a buffer that would preserve Republicans’ slim U.S. House majority. Trump’s push for the Texas map kicked off a tit-for-tat redistricting war across the country, producing similarly skewed maps in a number of states.

After Texas, Republicans were most hopeful to flip four Democratic seats they redrew in Florida. Three of them stayed blue, and the other was within a one-point margin. In California, where Democrats retaliated with new congressional maps of their own, they had picked up three of the five they targeted and were leading in the remaining two.

With GOP-leaning congressional maps powerless in the face of the blue wave, Democrats won the U.S. House and are set to have a substantial majority.The party has also wrested control of the U.S. Senate, leaving Trump to reckon with a Congress under full Democratic control for his last two years in office.

Under less dramatic circumstances, a number of new faces will join the ranks of Texas’ congressional delegation to replace ten U.S. representatives who are either retiring, gave up their seats to run for other offices or lost their primaries for reelection. Most of the races were in noncompetitive general election districts.

Two sitting representatives ran for U.S. Senate but lost in their respective primaries: Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Dallas, fell to James Talarico while GOP Rep. Wesley Hunt, R-Houston, finished behind Sen. John Cornyn and Ken Paxton.

Reverend Frederick Haynes III won Crockett’s endorsement to succeed her in the heavily Democratic 30th District. A Dallas native, Haynes has been pastor of the city’s Friendship-West Baptist Church for more than 40 years. He sailed his way into Congress in the deep blue district Tuesday.

Mortgage loan officer Jon Bonck will succeed Hunt in the safely red 38th District. Bonck received endorsements from Trump, Sen. Ted Cruz and other influential Republicans leading up to his victory in the general election.

The tenure of Rep. Chip Roy will also come to an end in January after the congressman ran for Texas attorney general, a contest he lost in a primary runoff to Mayes Middleton. This election left the staunchly Republican 21st District in the hands of Mark Teixeira, a former professional baseball player who started his 14-season Major League career as the fifth overall draft pick for the Texas Rangers in 2001.

And one incumbent, Rep. Dan Crenshaw, was forced into an early exit from his safe Republican seat by his primary rival, state Rep. Steve Toth of Conroe. The business owner defeated investment banker and Democratic nominee Shaun Finnie, and will be joining the U.S. House after five total terms, including the last eight years, as a state legislator.

Among the six soon-to-be retirees, two are Democrats. The seats of Reps. Lloyd Doggett and Marc Veasey will be filled, respectively, by Rep. Greg Casar, who ran for Doggett’s Austin seat after his own district was scrambled, and former Rep. Colin Allred. Both are returning to Congress — Allred after two years out of office — in new districts.

A new cast of Republicans will take over in four other safe districts.

Five-term Rep. Jodey Arrington will leave his seat to Tom Sell, who worked in the office of former Rep. Larry Combest. Sell worked at a law firm he founded with Combest before running for the U.S. House.

Rep. Michael McCaul will be succeeded by Chris Gober, who, before running for office, worked as the chief lawyer of Elon Musk’s America PAC that has channeled $216 million toward Republicans this cycle.

Rep. Morgan Luttrell also chose not to run for reelection after two terms. That opened the door for Jessica Steinmann, an attorney who previously worked in Cruz’s office as well as in the first Trump administration’s Department of Justice.

And a deceptively familiar face will replace Rep. Troy Nehls – that of his identical twin brother, Trever Nehls, who served in the U.S. Army for more than three decades and retired from the military as a Colonel. He’ll represent the Houston-area 22nd Congressional District.

This article first appeared on The Texas Tribune.

#6147. Angie Nixon could have won Florida. National Democrats failed her

Election Day brought a big blue earthquake of anti-Trump sentiment that rumbled as far inland as Kansas and shook GOP ground in the Carolinas and Texas. By the time late victories rolled in on Tuesday night, there had been so many wins that subsequent Democratic pickups had begun to feel more like aftershocks, even in states that havenât voted blue since Bill Clinton was in the White House.

Florida narrowly missed the quake, with Republicans winning all the major statewide races by the thinnest of margins. The one-time quintessential purple state, a so-goes-the-nation bellwether with a relatively even amount of registered Republicans and Democrats, turned remarkably red in the Trump era following Barack Obamaâs back-to-back wins in 2008 and 2012. The state legislature redrew its maps to enshrine a supermajority, and a post-Covid influx of GOP transplants seeking lower taxes and lax regulations shifted the balance significantly. A Democrat hasnât made a fight of the governorâs race this decade, and no Democratic Senate candidate has come close to winning since Bill Nelson lost his reelection bid in 2018.

Angie Nixon felt different. The Jacksonville organizer and bookstore owner ran a proudly democratic socialist campaign, advocating for universal healthcare in a state beset by multiple insurance crises and affordability issues. Her polls looked good up to Election Day, and on Tuesday night, victories across the country made her race in the Sunshine State look winnable. Ultimately though, Nixon could not replicate the victories of other rabble-rousers like Dr. Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and James Talarico in Texas. She lost to incumbent Ashley Moody, who was appointed by Gov. Ron DeSantis to fill the seat left vacant by Marco Rubioâs confirmation as secretary of state, by less than two percentage points. Moody outspent Nixon by more than double to barely eke out a majority.Â

The Florida Democratic Party deserves some blame for being woefully behind the times. After a 2019 squeaker between DeSantis and the progressive Andrew Gillum, the party moved as fast as it could from any candidate that might excite its base. They ran a former Republican for governor in each of the last two gubernatorial races, no doubt depressing turnout and enthusiasm among the Democratic base with their moderate picks.Â

But a close look at the rest of the Florida races reveals the culprit in Nixonâs narrow loss. Despite a gerrymander meant to calcify Republican supermajorities in the state and a political stiff in the form of David Jolly at the top of the ballot for governor, the GOP lost seats in the state legislature. The energy in Florida and, remarkably, throughout the South, was with anyone running against Republicans. The blame for Nixonâs defeat lies almost solely with national Democrats and their stubborn refusal to back Nixon with either messaging or money.Â

Since her shock primary win in August, Nixon has complained about Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee recalcitrance to anyone who will listen. In September, she told MS NOW hosts Symone Sanders Townsend and Eugene Daniels that Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer was less than thrilled about her race.

âWhen I did speak with Sen. Schumer on the phone, it was basically a âwe will see,ââ she said. âHeâs going to look into it. Thatâs what was said, that heâs going to look into it.â

Nixon went on to say that Democrats were wary of throwing in behind a Black woman in the South following Kamala Harrisâ 2024 loss: âFolks are a little gun-shy because, unfortunately, Vice President Harris lost as a Black woman, and so people are being very hesitant in terms of funding Black women, especially in the South.â

In later interviews, she claimed that national Democrats wrote off Florida in advance, declining to put money behind her candidacy because they believe the state is âracist.âÂ

The pale blue dots on Floridaâs election map tell the story. The democratic socialist was able to win in Miami-Dade County, despite a Cuban-American population that shudders at anything that sounds like revolution. On the other end of the state, typically Republican Jacksonville swung to the left. An enthusiastic push in the stateâs timidly liberal cities could have narrowed the gap in favor of Nixon and added tens of thousands of votes to her final total. According to analysis by Wesleyan Media Project, the national party and affiliated PACs spent 10 advertising dollars in Iowa for every one they spent in Florida in the raceâs final weeks, and it showed. The Hawkeye State now has a new Democratic governor-elect and senator-elect.

It was the same story throughout the South. Democrats overperformed in states where the national party bothered to fight.

It was the same story throughout the South. Democrats overperformed in states where the national party bothered to fight. Blue Texas became a reality because of seemingly unlimited spending â it was the most expensive Senate race in history âÂ and national messaging hits on behalf of Talarico. Louisiana and Mississippi offered two incredibly close Senate races in states long assumed to be GOP strongholds. In Louisiana, Democrat Jamie Davis lost to Republican Julia Letlow by only two points. As New York Times contributing opinion writer Steven Rattner pointed out, Davis kept the race close despite receiving zero advertising dollars from the national party in October, per the WMPâs analysis.

Mississippi, though, could turn out to be a miracle â in spite of the DSCC. With 96% of precincts reporting, Democrat Scott Colom, a district attorney, leads the incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by only 138 votes, with around 15,000 provisional ballots outstanding.

Speaking to Anderson Cooper on Wednesday, Mississippi state Rep. Cheikh Taylor, a Democrat, blamed the nail-biter on a lack of investment from the national party.

âEarly money always helps. Monies have come to the state of Mississippi, just not through the traditional means, though the DNC. We all know that the Colom campaign was locked out of that $30 million contribution to U.S. Senate races,â he said. âEven though the money didnât come, in Mississippi, we figure it out.â

Donât get me wrong. Colom, Davis and Nixon all deserve praise for their stunning performances, even if at least two of them came up short. Tuesday nightâs news offered a rare glimmer of hope in a bleak few years, but Democrats had a chance to permanently rebuke MAGA âÂ and instead they squandered it based on their own misconceptions about the South.

Grabbing two more close races via some well-placed funding for the partyâs nominees would have left them in a much better position to harry and harass the president and block his MAGA agenda over the next two years. All it would have taken was not capitulating in advance.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Africa Brief.

The highlights this week: A United Nations deadlock ends the 35-year-old peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara, local elections take place in South Africa, and Moscow tries to project an illusion of a successful Russia-Africa Summit.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Africa Brief.

The highlights this week: A United Nations deadlock ends the 35-year-old peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara, local elections take place in South Africa, and Moscow tries to project an illusion of a successful Russia-Africa Summit.

A deadlock between the United States and Russia at the United Nations Security Council on Friday ended a 35-year-old peacekeeping mission in the disputed African territory of Western Sahara.

The U.N. Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara, known as MINURSO, was established in 1991 to monitor a cease-fire after a 15-year armed conflict between Morocco, which claims sovereignty over the territory, and the Algeria-backed Polisario Front, which seeks Sahrawi independence. It was also tasked with organizing a referendum for Sahrawi self-determination.

The referendum has stalled for decades. Last month, a U.S. draft resolution for the Security Council sought to remove “referendum” from the mission’s name and make semi-autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty the sole basis for future political negotiations over Western Sahara. It would have also scaled back the peacekeeping force by April 2027.

Russia vetoed the plan, instead putting forth a rival proposal to grant the standard one-year extension without imposing terms that favored Morocco. That, in turn, was voted down by the United States. The mission’s mandate subsequently expired on Sunday.

Morocco annexed Western Sahara, a former Spanish colony, in 1975, displacing more than 100,000 people. An International Court of Justice ruling the same year found no historical basis for Morocco’s claim over the area. Rabat now controls around 80 percent of the territory, which boasts rich Atlantic fishing grounds and phosphate reserves.

Currently more than 160,000 Sahrawi refugees live in camps hosted by Algeria. International aid groups have denounced the U.N. Security Council’s failure to renew the mission and find a solution to the severe humanitarian crisis caused by the political stalemate.

Traditionally, Western powers maintained a neutral position on Western Sahara’s status. But in 2020, during U.S. President Donald Trump’s first term in office, Washington broke with precedent by recognizing Rabat’s sovereignty over the territory in exchange for Morocco reestablishing diplomatic relations with Israel under the Abraham Accords.

At the same time, Russia’s stance has been largely driven by its close geopolitical and economic alliance with Algeria, which backs the Sahrawi liberation movement.

The U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday, in which Democrats took control of both the House of Representatives and Senate, could eventually lead to a more nuanced stance from Washington on Western Sahara, especially since many Democrats have expressed support for the U.N.-led process. But any immediate reversal is unlikely.

Washington and Moscow have traded barbs in the wake of Friday’s deadlock. Mike Waltz, the U.S. ambassador to the U.N., said that Russia’s veto prevents “historic steps toward finally ending a 50-year conflict.” His Russian counterpart, Vassily Nebenzia, said the U.S. plan would have “set back the entire process of resolving the Western Sahara issue” by disregarding “a just, free and fair settlement based on the principle of self-determination.”

Sidi Omar, the Polisario Front’s U.N. representative, also warned that the U.S. resolution would “not only torpedo the foundations of the U.N. peace process but would also have set a very dangerous precedent that threatens broader regional and international peace and security.”

Some analysts have echoed these criticisms. “Eager for a quick diplomatic win,” wrote Hugh Lovatt, a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, Washington has “closed the space for negotiations and risks creating regional instability.”

A small U.N. team is now supervising a phased withdrawal of U.N. peacekeepers and the return of military vehicles and other assets to troop-contributing nations, including Egypt, Ghana, and Pakistan.

Security observers fear that MINURSO’s departure could lead to renewed fighting in the territory. Amid a security vacuum, some analysts fear Morocco may be emboldened to send in troops in a bid to grab more territory.

Wednesday, Nov. 4: South Africa holds local government elections.

Friday, Nov. 6: Zambian Finance Minister Situmbeko Musokotwane presents a delayed 2027 budget.

South African elections. Analysts are predicting that South Africa’s local elections on Wednesday will show growing political fragmentation. The country is already ruled by a coalition government after the African National Congress (ANC) lost its 30-year parliamentary majority in a historic general election in 2024.

A few days before the election, Trump announced that South Africa, the largest beneficiary of the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), would be removed from the duty-free trade agreement starting in January. But with less than 1 percent of South Africa’s total goods entering the U.S. market under AGOA, the decision will likely have little impact on the vote. Instead, domestic issues such as crime, corruption, and a lack of jobs are expected to be voters’ priority.

Voters will elect councils in all 257 municipalities, but a heavily indebted Johannesburg—the country’s biggest city—is the key battleground.

Johannesburg’s debt has spiraled in recent years, with consumer bills and other debt still owed to the city amounting to 72 billion rand (about $4.5 billion), with Johannesburg owing more than $1.5 billion to its immediate creditors. The city has struggled to collect trash and provide enough drinking water. By some estimates, nearly half of the city’s treated drinking water is lost to underground pipe leaks due to infrastructure neglect and commercial losses.

Currently, the white-led, pro-business Democratic Alliance (DA) is leading the pack in Johannesburg, where its former federal chairperson, Helen Zille, is campaigning for mayor. (Zille was also mayor of Cape Town from 2006 to 2009.)

Yet no party is predicted to win an outright majority. Most polls suggest the DA will win less than 40 percent of the vote in Johannesburg, followed by the ANC and two far-left parties: the uMkhonto weSizwe Party and Economic Freedom Fighters. The DA refuses to work with the latter two, which means it will likely form a coalition with the ANC or other smaller parties.

Déjà vu in Moscow. Moscow made a series of high-profile announcements around last week’s Russia-Africa Summit, including those concerning the sale of fighter jets to Ethiopia, Sudan’s offering of investment opportunities, and Russia’s support in modernizing Eritrea’s ports. Yet while some analysts have concluded that these evince Moscow’s rapidly growing role in Africa, there is reason to be skeptical.

None of these plans are new. Instead, Russia has highlighted and repackaged long-standing agreements to project an illusion of a successful summit. For instance, the delivery of 12 Russian Sukhoi Su-35 fighter jets and the planned acquisition of four S-400 air defense batteries to Ethiopia stem from a prior agreement signed several years ago; they are not, as the Moscow Times described it, “the summit’s highest-profile deal.”

Meanwhile, proposals for Moscow to modernize Eritrea’s ports have been floated since 2018. And Sudan, in order to secure military backing, has offered strategic cooperation with Moscow since the country’s civil war began in 2023.

At the summit, Moscow also announced nuclear power plant deals with several African nations, including Ghana. Yet apart from Egypt’s $29 billion El Dabaa project, decade-old nuclear power agreements between Russia and African nations remain unplanned. Russia agreed to build a nuclear plant for Ghana in 2015, for example, though it never came to fruition.

Congo mining dispute. California-based KoBold Metals, a mining start-up backed by Bill Gates and Jeff Bezos, has asked the United States for help in seeking U.N. Security Council approval to use aerial surveillance technology to map the location of critical minerals in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

The company accuses China of using a U.N. arms embargo—which blocks the supply of arms and related equipment to nongovernmental entities and individuals operating in Congo—to prevent it from using the technology, according to a Financial Times report. China has said the allegations are “inconsistent with the facts.”

Congo, the world’s largest exporter of cobalt, has faced decades of armed fighting over its mineral resources. Chinese companies currently control around 80 percent of the country’s cobalt output.

Sudan’s fragmented war. In Africa Is a Country, Doha Ali, who fled Sudan’s civil war, argues that framing the situation in the country simply as a “humanitarian crisis” flattens its complex history and obscures the foreign interventions and proxy dynamics, including European anti-migration policy, that established the conditions for endless warfare.

“Wars do not simply happen; they are built. Sometimes they are built through weapons. Sometimes through money. Sometimes through diplomatic agreements signed years before the first shot is fired,” Ali writes.

Ali’s article is part of the series We Are Here: Sudanese Girls and Youth Hold Their Ground in Resistance and Remembrance, a collection of stories by young Sudanese people documenting their lived experiences of war and displacement.

Egyptian media repression. On Oct. 27, an Egyptian court ordered the immediate closure of Mada Masr, one of the country’s last prominent independent news outlets, and fined its editor in chief, Lina Attalah, 3 million Egyptian pounds (around $53,450) for operating without a license. Attalah will soon face a criminal trial and possible imprisonment.

This forms part of a wider crackdown against independent news agencies in Egypt, which has detained or jailed more than 20 journalists. In New Lines Magazine, a Cairo-based journalist using the pseudonym Anne Mostafa details Egyptian authorities’ 13-year campaign against Mada Masr and what it means for the country.

Nosmot Gbadamosi is a multimedia journalist and the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly Africa Brief. She has reported on human rights, the environment, and sustainable development from across the African continent. X: @nosmotg

#6143. Meeks vows Iran votes as he seeks Foreign Affairs gavel

Rep. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., the presumed next chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, plans to bring resolutions to the floor to “immediately” end the war with Iran when Democrats take control of the House in January, he wrote in a letter Thursday seeking his colleagues’ support to become chairman.

The letter, which officially announced his bid for the chairmanship, lays out his oversight agenda for the committee, which will also see considerable turnover on the GOP side of the dais.

Meeks and other Democrats have repeatedly forced votes this year on war powers resolutions seeking to end the Iran war, with a Meeks-sponsored one clearing both chambers of Congress.

But those resolutions have been nonbinding concurrent resolutions, since the 1973 War Powers Resolution only lays out a fast-track procedure the minority party can wield for concurrent resolutions in the House.

With a House majority, though, Democrats could bring binding joint resolutions to the floor.

Beyond war powers votes, Meeks also promised public hearings on the war. He also vowed hearings on a range of topics including the administration’s Venezuela policy and “repeated defiance of Congress’s constitutional authority over war powers and trade.”

“As chairman in the 120th Congress, oversight of this administration’s lawlessness and corruption will be at the top of the agenda,” Meeks wrote. “I will continue to advance a principled foreign policy grounded in our values, including support for Ukraine against Russian aggression.”

In addition to Iran measures, Meeks also promised legislation focused on “clawing back Congress’s proper role in the making of American foreign policy” and a State Department reauthorization bill that puts guardrails on the administration and protects career diplomats.

Meanwhile, the GOP side of the committee is poised to lose at least a dozen lawmakers — or about half of its members — next year between retirements and election losses.

The departures include longtime members such as former Chairman Michael McCaul, R-Texas, who opted not to seek reelection, and Rep. Scott Perry, R-Pa., the Freedom Caucus chair who lost his reelection race.

Several other Republican committee members remained locked in races that were still too close to call as of Thursday afternoon, according to The Associated Press, potentially gutting the GOP committee bench further. They include GOP Rep. Young Kim of California, the East Asia and Pacific Subcommittee chair who was trailing her in race against fellow California Republican Rep. Ken Calvert.

Rep. Christopher H. Smith, R-N.J., who chairs the Africa Subcommittee, lamented the turnover Thursday but predicted a lot of interest among remaining House Republicans to fill the void.

“There will be many who will want to be on it,” Smith told reporters. “We lost some really great people. Yesterday I can’t tell you how sad I was about friends who are now not coming back.”

#6142. Taika Waititi’s Instagram crash out is a Trumpian sore loss

For all the horrible things Donald Trump has wrought upon the world â and there are so, so many â heâs also taught us some important lessons. Trump is proof of several truths: A red-meat-and-stress-addled heart can withstand otherwise unthinkable conditions with the federal governmentâs medical secrets; reality television ruined the world; and, if weâre not careful, weâre all liable to become parodies of ourselves one day, crying about it online.

That latter bit is certainly true for filmmaker Taika Waititi, whose otherwise tacky-yet-progressive veneer cracked last weekend when he took to Instagram to condemn the poor reviews of his latest film, âKlara and the Sun.â After a torrent of bad press and worse box-office performance, the filmâs distributor, Sony, opted to scale back the movieâs wide release, reducing the sci-fi dramedyâs reach from 2,000 theaters nationwide to 800, most of which returned a meager profit. Never one to take his mediocrity on the chin, Waititi deflected the negativity outward, which, as we know, always paints someone in a good light!

Waititiâs childish outburst is straight from the MAGA playbook. And while refuting film critics isnât akin to Donald Trumpâs most damning sins, Waititiâs mockery is a symptom of a problem that wonât be washed away by one blue wave, no matter how sizable.

Waititi reposted a graphic claiming that âKlara and the Sunâ was âreboundingâ with a 78% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes, a 53-point gap from the filmâs 25% critics score. (For what itâs worth, neither number should ever be used to accurately measure a filmâs quality.) âI havenât read a review of anything aimed at me or my peers in 15 years,â Waititi captioned the post. âBut I do listen to the people . . . Letâs spare a thought for those sad, lost souls who couldnât achieve their dreams of becoming artists, and thus settled, and became critics. Irrelevant. Out of touch. Obsolete. In the bin.â

Reading Waititiâs emoji-peppered caption, I was surprised to find it so carelessly evoked the Trumpian crybaby approach to social media. Whether on X or his own Truth Social, Trumpâs favorite way of addressing critics and opponents has long been to toss out adjectives at will. Tack a âSAD!â at the end of Waititiâs caption, and it could easily pass for one of Trumpâs poetic musings. (If only Waititi had gone so far as to parrot my personal favorite Trump quip about Barney Frank by saying, âThe critics looked disgusting, nipples protruding, in front of my movie. Very very disrespectful.â)

Ironically, all those admonishments in Waititiâs caption are also fitting descriptors for the state of Donald Trumpâs agenda, the one imitated by his legions of Republican cronies spread out across America, hoping to be elected in Tuesdayâs midterms. But judging by the results, MAGAâs influence is waning fast. Seven Senate seats flipped, historically red states turned blue and a spate of monumental wins popped up nationwide. The MAGA bubble popped in real time. Americans have seen firsthand what little good fascist ideology does for the average, working-class person. And though the country may not become great again overnight, it appears the last 12 years of freefall have finally been suspended â at least for now.

Not to be all, âOh, wonât someone think of the celebrities?â about it, but such overwhelmingly positive election results left me wondering what happens to someone like Waititi, whose childish outburst is straight from the MAGA playbook. For over a decade, Trump has used social media to peddle broadly disparaging, dangerous rhetoric that has legitimate impact outside the phone screen. The reckless hatred comprising MAGA ideology is so potent that itâs bled into the ways even otherwise progressive people wield their power, like crude oil painting an ocean black. And while refuting film critics isnât akin to Trumpâs most damning sins, Waititiâs mockery is a symptom of a problem that wonât be washed away by one blue wave, no matter how sizable.

One would think that Waititi would know better. For one, the guy is 51 years old, certainly experienced and well-established enough to let a flop roll off his back. How fitting that his biggest success is the anti-fascist yet aesthetically tasteless political satire, âJojo Rabbit,â which won the Oscar for best adapted screenplay in 2020, just as the Trump era was revving up for its second leg. That film, about a 10-year-old Hitler Youth who begins to grapple with the realities of life in 1940s Germany, examines propagandaâs influence and the power of hegemony, even if it often lacks the nuance and perspective such a satire warrants. For better, or more often, for worse, Waititiâs writing displays a self-possessed vulgarity that gets in the way of his more salient observations. Case in point: Itâs downright ludicrous to stake your name on a film renouncing hate, then take aim at critics â people not exactly matched in influence to someone like Waititi â just six years later.

But this is the rot that social media creates. Whether itâs Instagram, X, TikTok, or YouTube, these sites have incentivized and monetized incendiary opinions. Their algorithms push small people into major power. What was designed to ostensibly be a great equalizer has only divided the world more, making animosity easily accessible to anyone who gets their rocks off on sewing discourse through cruelty.Â

For some time now, arts critics have been easy targets on these platforms. Gone are the days of the critic playing dilettante, having intellectual conversations over martinis and cigarettes at the monthâs salon for like-minded individuals. To be a critic today â to pursue oneâs passion for art and writing and learning, all rolled into one â is to subject oneself to a pretty bleak existence. In most cases, the pay is meager. The hours are long. The job is demanding. And virtually no one has the patience or attention span to read an entire article anymore, let alone engage with its ideas. A legitimate critic doesnât stumble into the job just to point and laugh; they write because they have real passion for what they cover. Surely someone like Waititi would say the same when he begins a new project after a string of flops.

If living in MAGA-world for a decade has taught us anything, itâs that things arenât just good because one person says so. Uniformity is the enemy of art, and blind trust is the scourge of politics. There is no future without recognizing the subtleties existing between the lines.

What Waititi fails to realize is that heâs not punching up or down, but laterally. This is artist versus artist. If the context is right, a good piece of criticism can be as life-altering as a good film. But thatâs hard to see when the internet has built such a wide chasm between people, reducing the impact of writing in favor of scrolling. Along with social mediaâs effect on human behavior, itâs had a heavy hand in blunting the journalism industry. If everyoneâs a critic, then no one is, and thatâs precisely why monitoring Rotten Tomatoes scores like theyâre poll numbers is futile and ridiculous.

But itâs not just Waititi whoâs vulnerable to this unique form of MAGA-tinged, social media-brained psychosis; critics can fall prey to it, too. Whether itâs a filmmaker, a film critic, or just your average filmgoer, social media has confined us all to its machine. No one is exempt from consumer techâs sway. And if a writer or filmmaker wants to make a splash, tossing out an inflammatory opinion aimed at a peer is a surefire shortcut. Iâve seen this affect criticsâ prose over time, with certain writers (or their outlets) favoring button-pushing pull quotes and headlines for attention. But in most cases, no critic is happy to spend two hours watching something they find insufferable. No matter how gleeful Siskel and Ebert used to look sparring over movies, their industry was built on intellectual debate in pursuit of cinematic resonance, not schadenfreude.

Whatâs most concerning in Waititiâs response is his foul self-importance, which is the real stain of MAGA politics. While an artist should avoid burdening themselves with hypothetical responses to their work before itâs even out in the world, considering the eventual reaction is worthwhile. Engaging with other peopleâs perceptions is a practice we could all stand to do with more grace and tact. Contemplating a differing opinion shows maturity and humility, not absolute agreement. Pointing a finger wonât do anything for a personâs growth, artistic or otherwise. Americaâs politicians are only just beginning to relearn that lesson, understanding the value in trying to address problems, rather than gesture toward them with a shrug.

If Americaâs blue wave is indeed going to usher in a new era where politicians actually act in favor of the people, and Trumpian artists like Waititi make themselves look foolish on Mark Zuckerbergâs Instagram, we owe some props to one of the centuryâs most prolific liberals. Aaron Sorkinâs âThe Social Reckoningâ actually got a few things right. In last monthâs companion piece to âThe Social Network,â Sorkin posited that the average American would soon be mobilized by their fatigue with MAGA politics and social media. But his directorâs eye lacked style and discernment. Sorkin responded to criticisms with pleasant diplomacy, even questioning his own merits as a director versus a screenwriter. âIâm worried that the parts of directing that Iâm not good at are those parts you canât learn,â he admitted.

While there may be truth to his concern, Sorkinâs introspection is precisely the kind of pause this country could learn from. If living in MAGA-world for a decade has taught us anything, itâs that things arenât just good because one person says so. Uniformity is the enemy of art, and blind trust is the scourge of politics. There is no future without recognizing the subtleties existing between the lines. The only thing that is, to quote Waititi, irrelevant, out of touch and obsolete is the arrogance in thinking anyone could know it all.

#6140. Trump Has Shifted the U.S.-Pakistan Relationship

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

South Asia Brief: Trump Has Shifted the U.S.-Pakistan Relationship

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s South Asia Brief.

The highlights this week: A proposed liquefied natural gas project in Pakistan underscores close ties with the Trump administration, garment workers in Bangladesh protest for pay increases, and India’s opposition alliance rallies to call for the resignation of the chief election commissioner.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s South Asia Brief.

The highlights this week: A proposed liquefied natural gas project in Pakistan underscores close ties with the Trump administration, garment workers in Bangladesh protest for pay increases, and India’s opposition alliance rallies to call for the resignation of the chief election commissioner.

Since U.S. President Donald Trump returned to the White House last year, Pakistan has banked heavily on doing business with the United States. With the Democrats flipping both houses of Congress in the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday, though, one has to wonder if Islamabad could come out as another loser.

For one thing, scrutiny of Trump’s business dealings will certainly increase, constraining his administration’s capacity to pursue deals abroad.

A big topic of discussion in Pakistan this week—along with the midterms—is the news that a consortium of U.S. companies has proposed a $4.4 billion liquefied natural gas (LNG) project in Port Qasim, near Karachi. It would be Pakistan’s first LNG storage facility, helping to shield the country from global energy shocks.

The proposal entails a large-scale storage terminal and eventually a 680-mile delivery pipeline. The plan is backed by the U.S. Trade and Development Agency, U.S. International Development Finance Corp., and the Export-Import Bank of the United States.

Washington’s support for the proposed LNG project underscores just how much the U.S.-Pakistan relationship has changed in Trump’s second term. Bilateral ties were downgraded after the U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan in 2021, in large part because Washington had long viewed relations with Islamabad through a security lens.

The Trump administration turned this approach on its head. The United States now prioritizes ties with Pakistan, and Trump often praises the country’s leadership. Though counterterrorism still figures in the relationship, Washington has emphasized economic and commercial issues in its engagement with Islamabad.

In particular, the United States has taken a strong interest in Pakistan’s critical minerals and cryptocurrency resources. It has pushed for the country to import more U.S. goods, including energy supplies. In October 2025, Pakistan received its first-ever shipment of U.S. crude oil. Washington has pushed to remove trade obstacles with Islamabad, including ending a two-year ban on U.S. soybean exports.

Pakistan, which had long pitched its economic offerings to the United States unsuccessfully, has capitalized on the Trump administration’s newfound interest in its assets. The Financial Times reported last year that Islamabad went as far as to offer Washington the opportunity to build and manage a port on the Arabian Sea. (Pakistan publicly denies this.)

The proposed LNG project would be one of the Trump administration’s most ambitious commercial ventures in Pakistan, perhaps putting an exclamation point on the shift in the U.S. approach to the country. Yet that shift might not even be sustainable—especially given the midterm results.

The Trump administration’s commercial focus is largely driven by the president’s whims and by the economic interests of his family members and close associates. But this arrangement won’t outlast Trump’s term, which ends in two years. Further, with Congress in the hands of the Democrats starting in January, it could also become more difficult to pull off.

Conversations with Pakistani interlocutors this week revealed a combination of curiosity and concern about ties with the United States in the Trump era. There seems to be a desire to understand how the relationship improved so quickly alongside a sense that it might not last for long, given Trump’s unpredictability. The Democrats’ victory will only sharpen these concerns.

These worries reflect an evergreen challenge for the U.S.-Pakistan relationship: how to craft a strong partnership that can withstand political change in both countries and weather external shocks.

The last time the White House officially announced a policy on Pakistan was during Trump’s first term, in August 2017, when a new South Asia strategy included a hard-line approach toward Islamabad. It’s clear that the United States is overdue in conducting a formal review of its Pakistan policy, even as the relationship is being informally reevaluated and refashioned.

Garment protests in Bangladesh. Garment workers have taken to the streets in industrial areas of Dhaka, Bangladesh’s capital, in recent days to call for pay increases. Clashes with security forces have prompted the closure of dozens of garment factories and raised concerns about shipment delays.

Garment workers are a critical constituency in Bangladesh, numbering around 4 million, and the sector accounts for 80 percent of the country’s export earnings. Bangladesh’s ready-made garment industry is a global success story; it made the country one of South Asia’s best-performing economies until a slump in the last few years.

With the downturn, Bangladesh seems to be paying the price for relying so heavily on a single export—as globally competitive as it was—for so long. The protests are just the latest policy challenge for Dhaka, which is already struggling with economic stress, energy shortages, and the world’s most serious measles crisis.

These issues risk distracting Bangladesh from pursuing economic and governance reforms—something the government, which took office in February, was given a mandate to prioritize.

India’s opposition alliance rallies. On Sunday, the main opposition alliance in India staged protests in New Delhi to call for the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar. The rally drew tens of thousands of people and marked the latest mobilization against a voter roll revision that critics say favored the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party.

The youth-led Cockroach Janta Party has spearheaded the protests calling for Kumar to step down. This summer, the Cockroach movement galvanized protests over leaked exam papers that ultimately resulted in the resignation of the country’s education minister.

Now, India’s opposition is riding on the coattails of this activism. The success of the Cockroach movement is a gift to the opposition, which has long been hobbled by the absence of a popular leader and disagreements within its alliance.

Heat stress becomes serious vulnerability. The International Labor Organization (ILO) released studies last week warning that by 2040, workplace heat stress spawned by rising temperatures could lead to reduced working time equivalent to around 145,000 full-time jobs in Sri Lanka and 2,400 in the Maldives.

The reports estimate that these losses will be valued at around $26 billion in Sri Lanka and $576 million in the Maldives. The hardest-hit sector in Sri Lanka will be agriculture, along with services, manufacturing, and construction. In the Maldives, services and construction will be the most vulnerable industries.

The ILO findings are a reminder of the high economic cost of climate change in a region where economies are fragile—and where some of the most labor-dependent sectors are especially vulnerable to climate effects.

Last Sunday, around 200,000 people converged on the Bhutanese town of Gelephu to watch volunteers construct 108 stupas. (The number 108 is sacred in Buddhism.) The initiative is part of a campaign led by Bhutan’s king to transform Gelephu, near Bhutan’s border with India, into a “mindfulness city.”

Bhutan hopes to use the initiative, which emphasizes ecological sustainability and happiness, as an antidote to the country’s deepening economic stress. The stupa project is certainly an unorthodox way to tackle these problems. Critics will likely say it does little to reverse rising unemployment and a rapid outflow of highly skilled workers.

However, the project aligns with a long-standing Bhutanese principle known as “gross national happiness,” which measures national well-being not by income or other economic indicators but instead by the level of contentment among citizens.

Michael Kugelman is the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly South Asia Brief and a senior fellow for South Asia at the Atlantic Council. An analyst of the region for nearly two decades, he previously directed the South Asia Institute at the Wilson Center. X: @michaelkugelman

#6137. The grocery store shortcuts that make weeknight dinners easier

A version of this recipe first appeared in The Bite, Salon's food newsletter. Sign up for early access to articles like this, plus recipes, food-related pop culture recommendations and conversations about what we're eating, how and why.

There is a particular little sequence to my autumn evenings that Iâve come to adore.

I finish work, head to a dance class or the gym, and come home ready to cook. I pour myself a little cooking-time spritz â my current favorite is ginger-flavored sparkling water mixed with iced green tea and a squeeze of lemon â put on an old sitcom Halloween episode and open the refrigerator to see what weâre working with.

I love this part of the day. I love gathering ingredients, turning on the stove, deciding what sounds good. I especially love sitting down to something delicious afterward, knowing Iâve fed the muscles I just worked.

What I donât particularly love? Dirtying three separate bowls to bread chicken cutlets on a Tuesday night. Or peeling and chopping a pile of vegetables when Iâm already hungry. Or washing an enormous stack of dishes by hand, which has become an especially relevant consideration since my dishwasher gave up the ghost over the summer (and its replacement is currently in apartment maintenance limbo).Â

Which brings me to one of my more firmly held beliefs about home cooking: We canât be domestic goddesses for everything, you know?

And over the past several months, Iâve received a handful of emails from readers asking what packaged, prepared and otherwise convenient foods I actually buy. As it turns out, I have surprisingly strong opinions about groceries.

So, a little disclosure before we get into it: Nobody is paying me to recommend these products, and neither Salon nor I will earn money from these recommendations. These are simply the things I buy, use and genuinely enjoy. Some are specific brands; others Iâll happily buy from whichever label happens to be on sale.

For me, eating well right now means a dinner that takes less than an hour, includes at least two vegetables and some protein, ideally gives me a little more fiber, doesnât leave the kitchen looking like a crime scene and, above all, tastes really, really good.

And if spending a little extra on a convenience ingredient keeps me from placing an impulsive takeout order? Well, thatâs a pretty good investment, too.

Hereâs whatâs earning its keep in my kitchen lately.

Whole Foods frozen fried garlic breaded chicken breast fillets: I cannot overstate my affection for these things. Frankly, theyâre better than the breaded cutlets I usually make myself, and they eliminate the entire flour-egg-breadcrumb production, along with its accompanying dishes. Iâll serve them over pasta and vegetables, chop them into Caesar wraps or turn them into absolutely gorgeous fried chicken sandwiches. A box in the freezer is several possible dinners.

Frozen miniature meatballs: Any brand, really! I love these little guys for their versatility. For a quick stroganoff-ish dinner, Iâll simmer them with mushrooms, frozen aromatics, a gravy packet and fresh thyme, then finish everything with sour cream. Spoon the result over egg noodles, mashed potatoes or rice. Theyâre also excellent browned and added to Mediterranean-inspired bowls with rice, lemon hummus, feta, olives and a chopped cucumber-tomato salad. And when I want something comforting, Iâll toss them into pastina with finely diced vegetables for what I think of as âtiny everything soup.â

Heyday Canning Saucy Beans: Oh, how I love these. The beans come swimming in almost velvety sauces that are good enough that Iâd aspire to make them myself. The cans suggest simply heating and eating, which I wholeheartedly endorse. In fact, Iâve been known to sneak a cold bite of the tomato alla vodka beans straight from the can. No regrets. That variety is especially good as the foundation for a cozy skillet dinner, while the enchilada-flavored beans are excellent warmed and spooned over a rice bowl.

Laoban Popcorn Chicken with Soy Garlic Sauce: This freezer find really does scratch the takeout itch. The chicken pieces cook up light and crisp, while the sauce is a little bit of sticky heaven. I love serving them over rice with whatever vegetables I have waiting in the freezer, perhaps some steamed edamame, corn and shredded cabbage.

Jennyâs Tofu Organic Smoked Five Spice Tofu: Jennyâs tofu is made about 10 minutes from my Chicago apartment, and interviewing Jenny herself a few years ago helped convince me that many people who think they dislike tofu have simply never had really good, fresh tofu. The smoked variety is particularly wonderful for sandwiches. I love a barbecue smoked-tofu wrap with shredded red cabbage and corn relish, or a bÃ¡nh mÃ¬-inspired sandwich with crunchy vegetables.

Frozen scallion pancakes: Again, Iâm not especially brand-loyal. I like to treat these almost like tostadas, crisping them up and piling them high with toppings. One favorite is a sesame-scented chicken salad made with Kewpie mayonnaise, plenty of scallions and a little sesame oil. Spoon that over a hot scallion pancake for a delightful contrast of crisp, creamy and savory.

I once heard a piece of advice about eating more vegetables that Iâve never forgotten, although I wish I could remember who said it: Find the vegetables you can add to a meal almost automatically. The ones that make you say, âWhy the hell not?â

For me, those are pre-shredded cabbage and carrots.

Pre-shredded red and green cabbage: I put this on practically everything. Tacos, rice bowls, steak chili, prepared grain salads â anything that could benefit from a little crunch, color or freshness. I also love tossing green cabbage with miso butter, roasting it until the edges begin to brown, and finishing it with lemony, toasted panko breadcrumbs. Itâs inexpensive, keeps beautifully in the refrigerator and requires very little effort to turn into something special.

Pre-shredded carrots: These get tossed into stew bases, pasta sauces and curries, particularly anything Iâm planning to blend. Theyâre also the foundation of my current obsession: hibachi-style carrot-ginger dressing, which becomes almost laughably easy when you use frozen ginger and onion cubes, too.

Then thereâs my increasingly substantial frozen vegetable collection.

Fire-roasted corn, peas and carrots, mixed vegetables, edamame, spinach and cubed butternut squash: These are all regulars in my freezer. A note: Frozen vegetables are best with a little love. Iâll make compound butter to toss with them before roasting, whip up a herby sauce to coat them after steaming or finish them with a drizzle of brown butter, which is, in my opinion, king of nearly everything.

Iâve also become a fan of using prepared specialty cheese spreads to make indulgent broccoli. Break the florets â fresh or frozen â into small pieces, coat them with a good cheese spread (smoked Gouda and whipped Asiago have both been winners), and bake until bubbly, adding breadcrumbs if you like.

The philosophy is pretty simple: Iâd rather spend my energy making vegetables taste wonderful than spend all that time chopping them.

Now, hereâs where Iâm willing to get a little spendy.

I will not pay a premium for a bag of frozen vegetables that Iâm going to zhush up anyway. Generic peas are perfectly fine by me.

But sauces, pastes, condiments, good jams? Thatâs another story.

Sauz Lemon Pepper Pesto: One of my current favorites. Itâs creamy, acidic and provides a really distinct little lift to almost anything I spoon it over. I love tossing it with cubetti pasta, peas and canned white beans for a quick pasta salad, but itâs also fantastic smeared on sourdough toast and piled with olive oil-marinated vegetables.

Sun-dried tomato pesto: Another little jar of concentrated goodness. I love its deep, savory tomato flavor in pasta, sandwiches and vegetables. It also happens to be a key player in one of my favorite semi-homemade chicken sandwiches, which weâll get to shortly.

Curry paste: A good curry paste is an invitation to improvise. Add protein, vegetables, some coconut milk or stock, and youâre already well on your way to something fragrant and satisfying.

Mekhala Lemongrass Turmeric Paste: Just this week, I stirred a spoonful into a soup base of frozen onions, garlic and ginger, then added coconut cream, frozen mushrooms, shredded carrots, leftover rice and shredded rotisserie chicken. I finished the bowls with scallions, salted roasted peanuts and lime. The paste gave the whole thing an aromatic depth that would have required considerably more shopping and chopping to achieve from scratch.

Pacific Foods chicken miso ramen broth: The foundation of one of my favorite recent semi-homemade dinners. I like to doctor it with a little additional miso and coconut cream for richness, then pile on noodles, protein, vegetables and toppings.

Brown or mushroom gravy packets: Listen. I know how to make gravy. I also know that sometimes a packet of gravy is exactly what a weeknight cottage pie or a skillet full of meatballs needs. There is absolutely no shame in that.

Frozen ginger, onion and garlic cubes: Perhaps the least glamorous but most indispensable items on this list. They eliminate chopping, cut down on dishes and make the first few minutes of cooking almost frictionless. Iâm happy to buy whichever brand happens to be available or on sale.

Of course, a grocery list is only so useful without a little inspiration. Here are five dinners that show how these ingredients make their way onto my table.

These arenât formal recipes. Think of them as invitations to improvise.

This one is a little more ambitious, but itâs an excellent example of how convenience ingredients can leave more room for creativity.

I started with Pacific Foods chicken miso ramen broth, adding extra miso and coconut cream for richness, then used chicken Iâd already grilled earlier in the week for protein.

While the broth heated, I tossed frozen mushrooms, ginger and onions with oil, soy sauce and red pepper flakes, then roasted everything until the edges were almost charred. I steamed frozen corn and edamame, and tossed a generous pile of shredded red cabbage with sesame oil.

Into the bowls went noodles, broth, chicken, vegetables and roasted toppings, along with soy sauce eggs Iâd marinated earlier that day. I served a salad with homemade carrot-ginger dressing alongside.

Not exactly a five-minute dinner, but a beautiful one. And because so much of the prep was already done, I could spend my time on the little details that made the meal feel special.

This is the dinner for when I want something cozy and substantial but do not want to peel a single potato.

Brown ground beef or chicken in a skillet with frozen onions, garlic and mushrooms. Once everything has developed some color, stir in a brown or mushroom gravy packet, a splash of stock and a generous quantity of frozen mixed vegetables.

Let the filling simmer until thick and savory, then transfer it to a baking dish (or keep it in an oven-safe skillet, if you have one). Spread deli-counter mashed potatoes over the top and bake until the filling is bubbling and the potatoes are golden in spots.

Hearty, comforting and full of vegetables, without having to peel, chop or mash a thing.

This is one of those dinners that started with a can and became something much more interesting.

I browned a little hot Italian sausage in a skillet, then added sun-dried tomatoes, a can of tomatoes, Heydayâs tomato alla vodka beans, a splash of cream and frozen spinach.

Everything simmered together into a rich, savory, slightly spicy skillet situation. I served it with toasted sourdough tips for scooping up all that lovely sauce.

The beans bring both flavor and fiber, the sausage adds richness and heat, and the spinach practically disappears into the sauce. I would happily eat this again tomorrow.

This is the sort of thing I love making when I want something fresh, bright and satisfying without spending much time at the stove.

Cook some small pasta â Iâm fond of cubetti here â and add frozen peas and carrots, cooking them just long enough to heat through. Drain, cool slightly and toss with canned white beans and a generous amount of Sauz Lemon Pepper Pesto.

You can eat it slightly warm or chill it for later. Either way, the creamy, lemony pesto ties everything together, while the vegetables and beans make the whole thing more substantial.

Sometimes you just need one very good sauce.

Remember those Whole Foods chicken cutlets I was raving about earlier? Hereâs one of my favorite things to do with them.

While the cutlets cook, toast some soft potato buns and make a quick lemon-garlic mayonnaise. I use Kewpie, into which I stir freshly grated lemon zest and one of those handy frozen minced-garlic cubes, thawed.

When the chicken is nearly done, melt a slice of Muenster cheese over each piece.

To assemble, spread sun-dried tomato pesto on one half of the bun and the lemon-garlic mayo on the other. Add the cheesy chicken cutlet, then pile on an almost unreasonable quantity of fresh arugula. My beloved shredded cabbage would also be wonderful here if youâre in the mood for extra crunch.

The result is creamy, tangy, savory, crunchy and a little peppery. Itâs the sort of sandwich Iâd happily pay a cute restaurant a slightly unreasonable amount of money to make for me.

Instead, Iâm standing in my own kitchen, feeling very pleased with myself.

#6135. Americans Care About Foreign Policy. Now Democrats Must Listen to Them.

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Argument: Americans Care About Foreign Policy. Now Democrats Must Listen to Them.

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

There is a trope of U.S. political journalism so time-tested as to nearly rise to the level of a verity: In making their choices, voters in the United States place little emphasis on foreign affairs. But yesterday’s overwhelming victory by opposition Democrats has proved that this falls well short of a rule.

One needn’t take this on my authority. On Wednesday morning, after picking through the disastrous results for his Republican Party, U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance posted on social media: “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. … [E]veryone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

There is a trope of U.S. political journalism so time-tested as to nearly rise to the level of a verity: In making their choices, voters in the United States place little emphasis on foreign affairs. But yesterday’s overwhelming victory by opposition Democrats has proved that this falls well short of a rule.

One needn’t take this on my authority. On Wednesday morning, after picking through the disastrous results for his Republican Party, U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance posted on social media: “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. … [E]veryone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

Vance was attributing a clarity to his boss that U.S. President Donald Trump has shied from exhibiting on the United States and Israel’s ill-conceived and poorly executed war against Iran, which many observers believe was largely inspired by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The Israeli leader has long sought to persuade U.S. presidents to attack Iran, and in Trump, he finally found a willing—or gullible—partner.

As is well understood by now, Trump and Netanyahu’s war against Iran failed according to nearly all of its many shifting rationales. It did not destroy Iran’s Islamic system of government. It did not permanently defeat Tehran’s regional ambitions and may not even have downsized them. Iran still maintains extensive control over the supply of oil to global markets through the Strait of Hormuz, and its Yemeni allies, the Houthis, have demonstrated not just persistence but surprising prowess in attacking Saudi Arabia and other key Arab allies and arms clients of the United States.

But this is only the beginning of the pain that this war has incurred for the United States. Perhaps the single biggest factor in the elections, it has driven up U.S. gasoline and diesel prices far above their prewar levels, and in doing so, it has stoked inflation and driven up interest rates, creating hardship for tens of millions of Americans.

Skeptics may say this simply confirms the old wisdom that Americans only care about foreign affairs when it costs them money. But that is a distinction without much difference. Voters were not confused about the cause of their hardship. As Vance himself acknowledged, they knew it was the war.

This conflict, which was unquestionably a war of choice that many Americans see as having been unnecessary, has also badly depleted many of Washington’s most capable and expensive munitions, weakening its military posture in the world’s most sensitive theaters: the East China Sea and both Ukraine and NATO’s borderlands with Russia.

Combined with the extended deployment of aircraft carrier battle groups in the Middle East, this depletion has left both Taiwan and islands disputed between Beijing and Tokyo more vulnerable than at any time in recent memory to Chinese attack. Meanwhile, even if Trump were able to wake up from the trance that Russian President Vladimir Putin seems to have put him in, Washington now has far fewer of the advanced weapons systems that Kyiv desperately needs to defend itself from Moscow’s indiscriminate missile and drone attacks.

Beyond the midterms, foreign policy is likely to remain on center stage in the struggle between Trump and Congress over the next two years. Presidents who lose one or both chambers of Congress during midterm elections almost always face a sharp limitation in their powers. It is the rare administration that is able to pass any major domestic legislation under these circumstances. And so lame ducks tend to focus their energies on foreign policy, an arena in which the Constitution grants presidents tremendous sway.

At the same time, Democrats in the Senate and House of Representatives are unlikely to be able to pass any major reforms that the president will sign into law. Like Trump, these legislators may find that some of their greatest opportunities to affect U.S. policy and the country’s place in the world relate to international affairs.

Their first priority, given that it was a campaign promise across congressional races, will be to end the conflict with Iran. But how to do so from Capitol Hill? The answer lies in stringent control of the budget and enforcing the kind of accountability that was totally abandoned by the pliant, outgoing Republican Congress. Trump is seeking a vast increase in military spending, and the incoming Congress has the power to make sure that extending the war in Iran will not be funded.

This will not be easy. Congress has almost always found it difficult to resist new spending requests for the Pentagon. But this Congress, and its Democratic leaders, will be judged in good part on its ability to rein in Trump in the Middle East. That will require sorting through military appropriations with a fine-toothed comb and holding hearings that seek to extract clarity from the president’s military and foreign-policy appointees to an unaccustomed degree.

The bombastic and ill-prepared U.S. defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, is the most obvious target here. But Secretary of State Marco Rubio should receive equal attention. So far, he has been supremely slippery in terms of evading frank and detailed discussion of the Iran war, and that must end now.

If Iran sits atop the list of foreign-policy priorities for the new Congress, though, it nonetheless has serious competition. The Democrats can and must bring about badly needed accountability in other areas as well. Here, I’ll start with the United States’ increasingly grotesque collusion with Russia in its war on Ukraine. This has recently gone beyond limiting arms supplies to Kyiv and potentially hindering satellite intelligence through Elon Musk’s Starlink system that Ukraine badly needs for defense. Now, it includes casting a succession of economic lifelines to Moscow through oil deals with Russia and pressure on Europe to restore Russian energy supplies.

Congress will also have a vital role to play in achieving transparency in the White House’s smash-and-grab coup in Venezuela, in which it abducted a sitting president, installed a client to lead the country, and then secured opaque arrangements for Washington and U.S. private interests in Venezuela’s vast, if decrepit, oil industry.

More broadly, Trump has ridden roughshod over relations with advanced industrial allies all over the world, from Canada to Japan to South Korea. Meanwhile, he has turned the country’s back on the so-called developing world, displaying a crude disregard for the fellow humanity of people in poorer countries, many of whom once looked up to the United States. At a minimum, Congress must lay bare the sheer incoherence and self-destruction at work in these Trump policies in areas from economic growth to mutual defense to global public health.

Lastly, I come to Israel, not because it is the least of these topics, but because it may be the most difficult. Democrats will have to reckon with their own divisions before they can reckon with the wrongheadedness of overall U.S. foreign policy toward the country. Yet the time has come for the United States to stop indulging Israel’s worst behavior, including the genocidal atrocities of its campaign in Gaza and the settler violence and growing dispossession of Palestinians in the West Bank.

Trump himself tried to get ahead of this issue on the day of the election by saying that the United States will no longer massively underwrite Israel’s defense, as it has done for decades, and sell Israel the arms that it needs instead. But much more is required.

The United States has long been more a willing than unwitting partner of Israel in the destruction of Palestinian communities. It play-acted around dedication to a two-state solution for years prior to the Trump administration, which simply dropped the mask and ceased even pretending to care about the fate of Palestinians.

Democrats know that growing popular disenchantment with Israel’s heedless violence was a significant factor in this week’s victory. Now they must get over the notion, still popular in many quarters, that to forthrightly criticize Israel’s behavior and hold this long-standing U.S. ally to account constitutes antisemitism. In fact, treating Israel with respect demands this. And so will the preservation of the U.S.-Israeli alliance.

On Israel, as on Iran, voters have moved faster than the Washington consensus. The old truism held that Americans do not vote on foreign policy. This week they did, and the Democrats they elected should take them at their word.

#6133. How 4 states voted on election-related ballot measures

More than 100 statewide ballot measures went before voters this week, including a handful that could shape future elections in their states.

Here’s a look at how those measures fared, including one in Alaska that hasn’t been called as yet:

Voters in Maryland on Tuesday approved an amendment to the state’s constitution that will make it easier for the state’s Democrat-controlled legislature to redraw the congressional map for the 2028 elections.

The outcome was a victory for Democrats, who could potentially eliminate the state’s lone Republican-held seat – the 1st District on Maryland’s Eastern Shore, represented by Rep. Andy Harris, the chair of hard-line conservative House Freedom Caucus.

The Old Line State emerged as a bright spot in Democrats’ plan to counter the redistricting wars initiated by President Donald Trump and turbocharged by the spring Supreme Court ruling that diluted Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act and set off a slew of Republican-led map-remaking across the South.

But those GOP-led redistricting efforts appeared to backfire this week, with Democrats holding many of the redrawn seats in states such as Texas, Florida, Alabama and North Carolina.

Still, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore told reporters Wednesday that he was “ready to engage” with the legislature on a new map, citing the threat of further redistricting in Republican states.

“Donald Trump is not done. He has already been very clear about his intention to go after additional states, to go after places like Mississippi and South Carolina and Indiana,” Moore said, according to video posted by WBAL-TV 11 News.

Following an unsuccessful attempt to redraw the Maryland map in February, Moore called a special August legislative session during which state lawmakers voted to put the redistricting amendment, known as Question 3, on the November ballot.

The move faced immediate legal challenges from Republicans. Two Maryland courts ruled to block the measure from appearing on the ballot, finding that lawmakers had missed the legally imposed deadline to refer the ballot measure. The state’s Supreme Court, though, allowed the redistricting amendment to go before the voters, with changes to the ballot text.

State and national Democrats campaigned heavily for Question 3 as some public polling pointed to skepticism among voters. Former President Barack Obama even appeared in an ad urging voters to approve it.

Voters in the Show-Me State overwhelmingly rejected a Republican-drawn congressional map that sought to dismantle a safely Democratic seat in the Kansas City area.

Missouri Republicans enacted the new lines in 2025, aiming to give them an advantage in seven of the state’s eight House districts, including the 5th District held by Democrat Emanuel Cleaver II.

A protracted legal and political tussle over the map ensued.

The group People Not Politicians Missouri started a citizen petition to put the adoption of the map to a statewide vote. While the petition effort was pending, the state held its August primaries under the new lines. But in September, the state Supreme Court ruled that the 2025 map could not be used in the general election because of the pending ballot measure and ordered state officials to hold November’s election under the previous boundaries, first enacted in 2022.

Attempts to challenge the ruling in federal court ultimately proved unsuccessful, with the U.S. Supreme Court issuing an order that reinstated the 2022 map.

Groups on both sides of the ballot measure, known as Proposition A, reportedly spent millions to persuade voters. But St. Louis Public Radio reported last week that while opponents of the 2025 map were actively campaigning against it, organized efforts in favor of Proposition A appeared “nearly nonexistent.”

Republican efforts to try again and enact a new congressional map for 2028 could be complicated by a constitutional amendment, approved by voters Tuesday, that curtails the power of state legislators to override the result of a voter-approved initiative.

Voters in Massachusetts opted this week not to join states such as California and Washington and adopt a nonpartisan primary system.

The ballot initiative, known as Question 3, would have replaced the state’s partisan primaries with an open primary under which all candidates would appear on the same ballot, with the top two vote-getters, regardless of party, advancing to the general election.

The outcome was a victory for the chorus of labor unions and progressive groups, including the Working Families Party, that opposed the measure. Holding so-called jungle primaries, the groups argued, could make it harder for candidates without financial resources or high name recognition to run for office.

A bipartisan coalition that included the NAACP of New England and Republican former Gov. Charlie Baker supported the measure, arguing that open primaries would give voters more choice and create more competitive elections in a state dominated by Democrats.

Alaskans weighed in this year for the second time as many cycles on a ballot measure to revert to partisan primaries and repeal the state’s top-four ranked choice voting system.

With over 70 percent of the vote in, The Associated Press had yet to call the ballot initiative, known as Measure 2, which would also roll back certain campaign finance disclosure requirements. As of Thursday evening, the “no” side, which supports keeping the current election system, was narrowly ahead. The state has until Nov. 18 to finish counting outstanding ballots.

Under Alaska’s voting system, all candidates ran on the same ballot during the primary. Then the top four candidates, regardless of party, advance to the general election, which is decided by ranked choice voting if no one takes a majority of the vote.

In 2024, Alaska voters narrowly voted to keep the current system in place.

National Republicans, though, have largely opposed ranked choice voting, including President Donald Trump, who has characterized Alaska’s voting system as a “scam.”

The state’s use of open primaries and the top-four ranked choice system has drawn fresh scrutiny this year.  Outside groups spent big sums trying to boost underdog candidates during the Senate primary in an effort to hurt the front-runners. And several candidates in the Senate, House and governor’s races dropped out before the deadline to finalize the general election ballot, again trying to prevent splitting votes with their party front-runners.

Then last week, the Senate race was upended by a New York Times investigation that revealed operatives aligned with the Senate campaign of Democratic Mary Peltola helped recruit a candidate with a similar name to her opponent, Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in an attempt to stack the four-candidate ballot with two Republicans with the same first and last names. The revelations have fueled an ongoing debate there about whether ranked choice voting encourages this kind of campaign chicanery.

“We would not be having this conversation at all if we didn’t have a thing in place called ranked choice voting,” Mike Dunleavy, Alaska’s outgoing Republican governor, told Fox News last week.

Dunleavy has ordered an investigation into the revelations, as has the Justice Department. The DOJ also sought to block the certification of the state’s Senate results if the incumbent Sullivan loses. Last weekend, a federal court dismissed the lawsuit.

Alaska and Maine are the only two states that currently use ranked choice voting in regular federal elections, along with the District of Columbia.

Michael Macagnone contributed to this report.
